$note: P06's stitching layer. Every node and every link is authored, dated and sourced. NOTHING in this file is computed: there is no routing, no reachability, no sailing time and no counterfactual. A link is a real cable segment or a real scheduled steamer route, and `fromYear` is the year that segment opened. Where a source disagrees with another about a year, the note says so. Unit ids are from app/data/geo/units.index.json and are never invented.

headrick-1991.author: Daniel R. Headrick
headrick-1991.work: The Invisible Weapon: Telecommunications and International Politics, 1851–1945
headrick-1991.supports: The submarine cable network, its chronology, its ownership and the strategy of an all-British route.

headrick-1981.author: Daniel R. Headrick
headrick-1981.work: The Tools of Empire: Technology and European Imperialism in the Nineteenth Century
headrick-1981.supports: Steamships, coal and the telegraph as the physical conditions of nineteenth-century empire.

kennedy-1971.author: P. M. Kennedy
kennedy-1971.supports: The strategic argument for cables touching only British soil, and the Pacific Cable of 1902.

harcourt-2006.author: Freda Harcourt
harcourt-2006.work: Flagships of Imperialism: The P&O Company and the Politics of Empire from Its Origins to 1867
harcourt-2006.supports: The mail and passenger route east, the contracts that paid for it, and the coaling stations it required.

carnarvon-1882.author: Royal Commission on the Defence of British Possessions and Commerce Abroad
carnarvon-1882.supports: The list of coaling stations Britain judged it had to hold and fortify, and why.

nodes.name: Porthcurno and the Thames
nodes.note: Nearly every cable east and south of Britain landed at Porthcurno in Cornwall, which by 1918 was the largest cable station in the world.

nodes.name: Gibraltar
nodes.note: The gate of the Mediterranean, taken in 1704 and fortified ever since; a cable relay from 1870 and a coaling station on every eastern route.

nodes.name: Malta
nodes.note: Grand Harbour: the Mediterranean fleet's base, a coaling station and a cable relay.

nodes.name: The Suez Canal
nodes.note: Opened November 1869. It cut the distance from London to Bombay by roughly two fifths and made everything east of it a British strategic problem.

nodes.name: Aden
nodes.note: Taken in 1839 to coal the steamers to India, and held for 128 years for the same reason.

nodes.name: Perim
nodes.note: An island in the strait at the mouth of the Red Sea, occupied to close it.

nodes.name: Colombo and Galle, Ceylon
nodes.note: The junction of the routes to India, Australia and China; the mail steamers coaled here.

nodes.name: Singapore
nodes.note: The pivot of the eastern seas: a free port from 1819, a cable junction from 1870, a naval base from 1923 — and surrendered in February 1942.

nodes.name: Hong Kong
nodes.note: The terminus of the China cable and the base of the China Station.

nodes.name: Penang
nodes.note: The first British station in the straits, and a cable relay on the Madras–Singapore segment.

nodes.name: Labuan
nodes.note: Taken for its coal seams, to fuel steamers in the China seas.

nodes.name: Mauritius
nodes.note: The Indian Ocean staging post on the Cape route, taken from France in 1810.

nodes.name: St Helena
nodes.note: A Company island in the middle of the South Atlantic, on the Cape route, and a cable station from 1899.

nodes.name: Ascension
nodes.note: Occupied in 1815 to watch Napoleon on St Helena, then kept as a victualling and cable station. Run for decades as if it were a ship.

nodes.name: Simon's Town, the Cape
nodes.note: The route to India before Suez, and the fallback after it.

nodes.name: The Falkland Islands
nodes.note: The South Atlantic station on the Cape Horn route, and the reason a British squadron was in the South Atlantic in 1914.

nodes.name: Bermuda
nodes.note: The dockyard that watched North America after 1783.

nodes.name: Freetown
nodes.note: The West African station: the base of the anti-slave-trade squadron, then a coaling stop and a cable relay.

nodes.name: Zanzibar
nodes.note: The East African relay on the Aden–Durban cable.

nodes.name: Cocos (Keeling) Islands
nodes.note: A cable station on two coral islets, and the reason the German cruiser Emden came here in November 1914 and was destroyed.

nodes.name: Fanning Island
nodes.note: An uninhabited atoll annexed so that the Pacific Cable could cross seven thousand kilometres of ocean without touching foreign soil.

nodes.name: Suva, Fiji
nodes.note: The mid-Pacific relay of the 1902 cable.

nodes.name: Norfolk Island
nodes.note: Where the Pacific Cable divided for Queensland and New Zealand.

nodes.name: Bamfield, Vancouver Island
nodes.note: The Pacific Cable's eastern end, reached overland across Canada.

nodes.name: Heart's Content, Newfoundland
nodes.note: Where the first working Atlantic cable came ashore in July 1866.

nodes.name: Bombay
nodes.note: The eastern end of the 1870 cable. A message from London reached the Government of India the same day; before it, the answer to a question took four months.

nodes.name: Madras
nodes.note: Where the cable east to Penang and Singapore began.

nodes.name: Darwin
nodes.note: The Java cable came ashore here in November 1871 and waited nine months for the Overland Telegraph to reach it.

nodes.name: Adelaide
nodes.note: The southern end of the Overland Telegraph, completed on 22 August 1872.

nodes.name: Southport, Queensland
nodes.note: The Australian landfall of the Pacific Cable.

nodes.name: New Zealand
nodes.note: Joined to Sydney by cable in 1876, and to Canada by the Pacific Cable in 1902.

nodes.name: Sydney
nodes.note: On the line from Adelaide, and the Australian end of the 1876 New Zealand cable.

nodes.name: Valentia Island
nodes.note: The European end of the Atlantic cable, on the Kerry coast.

nodes.name: Durban
nodes.note: The southern end of the East African cable of 1879.

nodes.name: Alexandria and Suez
nodes.note: The hinge of the whole eastern system, cable and canal both — which is a large part of why Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 and stayed 74 years.

nodes.name: Cyprus
nodes.note: Taken on lease from the Ottoman Empire in 1878 as a place of arms for the eastern Mediterranean; two base areas are still British.

nodes.name: Port Mahon, Minorca
nodes.note: Britain's Mediterranean base before Malta, held three separate times and given up for good in 1802.

links.note: The Atlantic cable. Two failed attempts in 1857 and 1858 and one broken cable in 1865 came before it.
Porthcurno to Gibraltar, with a relay on the Portuguese coast.
Malta to Alexandria.
Suez to Aden, down the Red Sea.
Aden to Bombay, opened in 1870. London to Calcutta went from four months by ship to a working day.
By way of Saigon.
Singapore to Java to Darwin. The cable was working in November 1871; there was nothing at the Darwin end to connect it to until August 1872.
The Australian Overland Telegraph: 3,200 kilometres of pole and wire across the centre of the continent, on land taken from Arrernte, Warumungu and Larrakia people, completed 22 August 1872.
The existing colonial land lines.
The East African cable, laid down the coast.
Zanzibar to Durban, by way of Mozambique.
The West African coast cable reached Cape Town in 1889, so the Cape could be reached without the Red Sea.
By way of Madeira and the Cape Verde Islands, which were Portuguese — one of the foreign landings the 1902 Pacific route was built to avoid.
Two volcanic rocks in the South Atlantic, wired together because they were the only British ground between Africa and Brazil.
The longest single cable span then laid, Bamfield to Fanning Island.
Completing the All Red Line: a telegraph loop around the world touching no soil that was not British.
By way of Batavia.
The P&O mail route east, under a Post Office contract: Southampton to Gibraltar.
To Alexandria. Until 1869 passengers and mail crossed to Suez overland and joined a second ship.
Down the Red Sea. Aden was taken in 1839 to put coal at the far end of it.
Aden to Galle and Colombo, where the routes to Calcutta, Australia and China divided.
The old route east, before the canal: down the Atlantic to the South Atlantic islands.
The Cape route to India. Four to six months out; the Suez route did it in three weeks.
